context: State-Wise & Variety-Wise Market Availability Calendar

Over 85% of India’s potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) harvest originates from the winter (Rabi) season across the Indo-Gangetic plains. The fresh crop hits wholesale markets between late November and March, followed by a 9-month cold-storage liquidation cycle (April through November) that stabilizes domestic availability until the subsequent winter harvest.
Key Table Varieties & Belts (Domestic & Export Footprint)

India exports between 400,000 and 550,000 MT of fresh table potatoes annually. Shipments are concentrated in oval/round white tubers (low reducing sugars, medium specific gravity) and red-skinned varieties entering regional South Asian and Middle Eastern corridors.
Key Processed Products & Production Breakdown Estimates

Industrial processing absorbs approximately 9.0% to 11.5% of India's total potato production (roughly 5.2 to 6.5 million MT of fresh tubers annually). Processors require specialized agronomic parameters to prevent the non-enzymatic Maillard reaction (caramelization of reducing sugars with amino acids during high-temperature frying, causing dark brown or black discoloration).
Industrial Potato Chips & Crisps: Thinly sliced (1.2–1.5 mm) rounds fried in palm olein or sunflower oil. Requires cultivars with reducing sugars  (glucose and fructose) and high specific gravity ().

Frozen French Fries & Specialty Extruded Shapes: Long-cut fries, hash browns, and potato wedges flash-fried and blast-frozen at  for retail and quick-service restaurant (QSR) chains (e.g., McDonald's, Burger King, KFC). Requires long-oval/cylindrical tubers ( length), shallow eyes, and dry matter .

Dehydrated Potato Flakes & Granules: Cooked, drum-dried potato sheets milled into fine flakes; base ingredient for extruded snacks (e.g., Lay’s Stax, Haldiram’s bhujia/namkeen), soup thickeners, and bakery binders.
Potato Starch (Farina): Wet-milled, centrifuged native starch for industrial papermaking, textile sizing, and processed meat binders.
Canned Baby Potatoes: Small calibrated tubers () vacuum-sealed in brine for export and institutional hospitality catering.

Crop Phenology & Climatic Parameters

Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a cool-season herbaceous annual. Commercial production relies on distinct photoperiod and temperature triggers: vegetative foliage development favors 20–25°C, whereas tuber initiation and starch bulking strictly require cool night temperatures (15–18°C). Tuberization slows dramatically above 21°C and stops completely above 28°C.
Sprouting & Emergence           Stolon Emergence & Initiation        Tuber Bulking & Cell Expansion       De-haulming & Skin Curing          Harvest & Cold Storage
Apical Bud Sprout                   Lateral Stolon Hooking                   Linear Weight Gain                    Foliage Chopping / Cut               Drying & Sorting
Root Anchor Establishment           Ovary/Tuber Sizing (Marble)              Dry Matter & Starch Accumulation      Periderm Suberization (Setting)      Ambient Curing / Store
Detailed Phenological Breakdown
Sprouting & Plant Emergence Phase (Day 0 – 20)
Phenology: Pre-sprouted certified seed tubers (35–45 mm, 40–50 g) planted in ridges and furrows; sprouts emerge through soil crust; adventitious fibrous root system anchors beneath seed piece.
Ideal Climate: Soil temperature 18–24°C; moist, friable, well-aerated sandy loam.
Agronomic Hazard: Excessive soil moisture or anaerobic conditions cause seed piece decay from Soft Rot (Pectobacterium).
Stolon Emergence & Tuber Induction (Day 21 – 40)
Phenology: Underground stems (stolons) elongate laterally from lower nodes; terminal tips swell and hook into rudimentary tubers (tuber initiation / "pea-to-marble" stage).

Critical Climatic Trigger: Low night temperatures (14–18°C) coupled with short photoperiods (8–10 hours) trigger high gibberellic acid reduction and activate the sucrose transporter enzyme StSP6A (tuberigen), inducing rapid tuberization.
Thermal Threat: Night temperatures  stimulate stolons to emerge above ground as vegetative shoots instead of setting tubers.
Tuber Bulking & Dry Matter Accumulation (Day 41 – 80)
Phenology: Cell division in tubers ceases; tubers expand purely through cell enlargement; rapid accumulation of starch, protein, and dry matter.
Ideal Climate: Daytime temperatures 20–24°C, cool night temperatures 10–14°C; uniform soil moisture tension (-25 to -35 kPa).
Agronomic Interventions: Earthing-up (hilling) at 30–35 days to bury developing stolons, preventing sunlight exposure that induces chlorophyll and toxic solanine glycoalkaloid formation ("greening").
De-haulming & Periderm Curing / Skin-Setting (Day 81 – 95)
Phenology: Vines naturally yellow and senesce; for seed crops and cold-storage table varieties, foliage is cut, pulled, or chemically desiccated (de-haulmed) using Paraquat / Diquat.

Physiological Purpose: Leaves the tubers underground for 10 to 15 days in dry soil; converts the thin epidermal layer into a tough, multi-layered suberized corky periderm (skin) resistant to scraping, feathering, and fungal infection during mechanical harvesting.
Harvest & Post-Harvest Curing (Day 96 – 110)
Phenology: Mechanical digging using elevator diggers; tubers cured in heaps at 15–20°C (85–90% RH) in shaded sheds for 7–10 days to heal micro-wounds before grading and bag packing.
Storage Regimes:
Seed Potatoes: Cooled gradually to 2°C–4°C (90–95% RH) to preserve dormancy.
Processing Potatoes: Stored at 8°C–10°C with CIPC fogging to prevent cold-induced sweetening (glucose accumulation).

The Indian onion (Allium cepa L.) economy operates across three distinct seasonal croppings: Kharif (10–15% of national volume), Late Kharif / Rangda (15–20%), and Rabi (65–70%). While Kharif and Late Kharif supply immediate fresh-market needs during autumn and winter, only the high-dry-matter Rabi crop is biologically suited for long-term storage in traditional ventilated structures (Kanda Chawls), sustaining India from June through October.

India exports between 1.6 and 2.5 million MT of fresh onions annually, making it one of the largest global fresh exporters. Shipments are strictly governed by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) using export duty, Minimum Export Price (MEP), or temporary prohibition levers to manage domestic retail food inflation.
Key Processed Products & Production Breakdown Estimates

India processes approximately 6.5% to 8.5% of its gross onion crop (roughly 1.8 to 2.5 million MT of fresh raw onions annually). Over 85% of processed volume is concentrated in dehydrated white onion production, making India the second-largest exporter of dehydrated onions in the world after the United States.

Dehydrated White Onion Flakes & Kibbled: Peeled, root-cored, washed, sliced (3–5 mm), and hot-air continuous belt-dried (down to moisture ); primary industrial format exported globally for seasoning, canned soups, prepared meals, and fast-food rehydration.

Dehydrated Onion Powder & Granules: Milled and air-classified fractions (powder, minced, chopped) derived from dehydrated flakes; basic ingredient in dry spice blends, bouillon cubes, instant noodles, and extruded snacks.
Dehydrated Red & Pink Onion Products: Processed in secondary volumes for ethnic spice mixes and barbecue sauces.

Frozen / Individually Quick Frozen (IQF) Diced Onions: Cleaned, diced (6 mm, 10 mm), and blast-frozen at ; supplied directly to domestic QSR chains, institutional foodservice, and ready-to-eat curry lines.
Onion Paste & Puree (Retort / Frozen): Mechanically ground raw or sautéed onion paste, thermally sterilized with citric acid preservation; base for shelf-stable wet gravies.
Onion Essential Oil & Oleoresin: Solvent- or steam-distilled volatile oil; utilized for pharmaceutical digestive tonics, topical hair-fall formulations, and industrial flavor compounding.

Crop Phenology & Climatic Parameters

Onion (Allium cepa) is a biennial herb grown commercially as an herbaceous cool-season annual. The plant exhibits distinct photoperiod and thermal triggers: vegetative leaf growth requires cool temperatures (13–24°C) and short days, while bulb initiation and maturity strictly require warm temperatures (25–35°C) and longer daylengths (10–12 hours for Indian short-day cultivars).
Nursery Seeding & Hardening       Transplanting & Establishment       Active Vegetative Growth          Bulb Initiation / "Swelling"       Neck Fall & Maturity
Protected Raised Beds                 Fibrous Root Anchor                   Leaf Sheath Thickening               Cell Enlargement              Pseudostem Softening
Seedling Stem: Pencil Size            Inter-Row Hoeing                      Photosynthetic Leaf Blade            Scale Filling / Wax Coat      Field Top Senescence
Detailed Phenological Breakdown
Nursery Phase & Seedling Hardening (Day 0 – 45)
Phenology: Seeds sown on raised nursery beds ( width); germination occurs in 6–8 days; seedlings produce 4–5 slender leaves.
Target Transplanting Caliber: Hardened seedlings must attain a pencil-thickness stem diameter (6–8 mm) and height of 15–20 cm.

Risk: Over-aged, thick seedlings ( diameter) experience vernalization under winter cold, causing undesirable premature bolting (formation of floral seed stalks), which ruins bulb quality. Under-sized seedlings suffer transplanting shock and poor establishment.
Transplanting & Root Establishment (Day 46 – 65)
Phenology: Seedlings transplanted into flat beds or broad bed furrows (BBF) at  spacing; adventitious fibrous root system anchors in the top 15–20 cm soil horizon.
Ideal Climate: 15–22°C; light, frequent irrigation to maintain continuous capillary moisture.
Vulnerabilities: Highly sensitive to damping off (Pythium, Rhizoctonia) and transplant wilting.
Active Vegetative Growth & Canopy Formation (Day 66 – 105)
Phenology: Rapid emergence of tubular, glaucous leaves with waxy cuticles (target: 8–10 fully functional leaves before bulbing begins); pseudostem (neck) thickens.
Ideal Climate: 18–25°C daytime; relative humidity 55–65%.
Biological Rule: Every functional leaf corresponds to one concentric fleshy ring (scale) inside the mature bulb; maximizing healthy leaf area directly governs final bulb diameter.
Bulb Initiation & Enlargement Phase (Day 106 – 135)

Phenology: Leaf blade emergence halts; photosynthates translocate downward to the base of the leaf sheaths, which swell into concentric fleshy storage scales; outer scales turn papery and develop variety-specific pigmentation (anthocyanin red or flavonol yellow).
Climatic Triggers: High solar radiation, temperature rising to 28–34°C, and photoperiods exceeding 10.5–11.5 hours.

Agronomic Management: Nitrogen fertigation must be stopped completely by Day 90–100; late nitrogen inputs delay bulb maturity, cause thick necks (bull-necks), and promote rots in storage. Potassium () and sulfur () application must peak to drive dry matter, skin tightness, and pungency.
Physiological Maturity & Neck Fall (Day 136 – 155)
Phenology: Cell division and expansion cease; the pseudostem right above the bulb hollows out and softens, causing the foliage to collapse onto the ground (neck fall).
Harvest Stage: Commercial harvesting begins when 50% to 70% of the field exhibits natural neck fall.
Curing Regimes:
Field Curing (Windrowing): Bulbs are left in field rows for 3–5 days with foliage covering bulbs to prevent sunscald.
Shade Curing: Foliage is cut leaving a 2.0–2.5 cm neck stub, and bulbs are cured in well-ventilated dry sheds for 10–15 days to allow outer skins to dry into parchment-like protective scales.

Unlike potato and onion, tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) is a delicate, perishable berry with an ambient post-harvest life of only 5 to 10 days. The national supply matrix runs on a bimodal seasonal engine: the Rabi crop (~60% of national volume, harvested December to April) and the Kharif / Late-Kharif crop (~40%, harvested August to November). The high-elevation microclimates of the Deccan plateau (Madanapalle, Kolar) and northern hill pockets (Solan) fill the critical monsoon deficit window (June to August).

Fresh tomato exports from India range between 120,000 and 180,000 MT annually, primarily moving via cross-border refrigerated land routes into neighboring South Asian nations and via air and short-sea reefer consignments into the Middle East.
Key Processed Products & Production Breakdown Estimates
Commercial processing absorbs approximately 1.2% to 1.8% of India's gross tomato production (roughly 250,000 to 380,000 MT of fresh fruit equivalents annually).

The primary industrial bottleneck is varietal: the vast majority of Indian acreage is planted with fresh table hybrids characterized by low Total Soluble Solids (TSS 4.0–4.5° Brix), thin flesh, high seed/water content, and low consistency. Industrial paste production requires dedicated processing-grade tomatoes with , high lycopene, thick pericarp, high Bostwick consistency (viscosity), and uniform red color without yellow shoulders.

Aseptic Tomato Paste (28° to 30° / 36° to 38° Brix Hot-Break): De-seeded, skin-separated, vacuum-concentrated paste packed in 215 kg aseptic bag-in-drum formats; industrial base for manufacturing ketchup, sauces, packaged soups, and snack flavorings. "Hot-break" processing () deactivates pectinolytic enzymes (polygalacturonase), preserving high pectin for viscous ketchup.
Aseptic Tomato Puree (12° to 14° Brix): Single-stage evaporated tomato pulp; retail and institutional culinary base for shelf-stable gravies and curries.
Tomato Ketchup & Culinary Table Sauces: Formulated emulsions combining 28° Brix paste with vinegar, sugar, salt, and spices; leading commercial retail processed category.

Canned Diced / Crushed Tomatoes (Peeled in Juice): Mechanically or steam-peeled firm, diced processing tomatoes packed in acidified tomato juice in sanitary tin cans for international hotel and restaurant (Horeca) pizza/pasta lines.
Dehydrated Tomato Powder & Flakes: Spray-dried or vacuum-belt-dried tomato solids used for instant soup mixes, extruded snack seasoning dusts (e.g., tomato wafers, puffs), and seasoning blends.

Crop Phenology & Climatic Parameters

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a day-neutral, warm-season herbaceous plant grown commercially as an annual. It requires warm, sunny days and cool nights: optimal daytime temperatures are 24–28°C, while night temperatures strictly require 15–20°C. Night temperatures falling below 13°C or rising above 27°C inhibit fruit set.

Detailed Phenological Breakdown
Nursery & Plug Tray Phase (Day 0 – 25)
Phenology: Seeds sown in 98-well plastic pro-trays filled with sterile cocopeat + perlite + vermiculite under 40-mesh insect-proof net houses. Seedlings develop 4–5 true leaves.
Ideal Climate: 25–28°C; relative humidity 65–75%.
Biosecurity Mandate: Protected net-house nurseries prevent early viruliferous whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) feeding, protecting crops from early Tomato Leaf Curl New Delhi Virus (ToLCNDV) infection.
Transplanting & Field Establishment (Day 26 – 40)

Phenology: Hardened seedlings planted into raised beds covered with 25–30 micron silver-black reflective plastic mulch with inline drip laterals ( spacing). Adventitious roots spread within the top 30 cm soil layer.
Management: Immediate establishment irrigation; installation of bamboo or GI wire trellis lines for staking indeterminate and semi-determinate hybrids.
Active Vegetative Growth & Branching (Day 41 – 60)
Phenology: Primary and secondary branch expansion; development of dense photosynthetic foliage; terminal flower clusters begin to differentiate.
Ideal Climate: 22–28°C; balanced nitrogen and phosphorus fertigation.

Trellising Intervention: Lateral shoots (suckers) below the first flower cluster are pruned out, and primary scaffold stems are tied with polypropylene twine to overhead horizontal wires (maintains open, vertical canopy).
Anthesis, Pollination & Initial Fruit Set (Day 61 – 80)
Phenology: Inflorescence clusters open; flowers are yellow, pendant, and hermaphroditic with connate anthers forming a protective cone around the pistil.
Pollination Biology: Self-pollinated, requiring physical vibration (buzz pollination by wind, bumblebees, or manual staking agitation) to dislodge pollen from anther pores onto the receptive stigma.
Critical Thermal Stress Thresholds:
High Heat Damage: Daytime temperatures  or night temperatures  cause style exertion (stigma sticks out past anther cone), pollen desiccation, and complete blossom drop.
Cold Damage: Night temperatures  cause pollen sterility and parthenocarpic, puffy, deformed fruit (cat-facing).
Fruit Bulking & Mature Green Stage (Day 81 – 110)

Phenology: Rapid cell division followed by continuous cell enlargement; locular cavities fill with jelly-like parenchymatous tissue; seeds mature and form protective mucilage coats; fruit reaches final physical size and turns pale green to whitish-green.
Nutrient Demand: Potassium () and Calcium () demands peak; fertigation shifts to a 1:1:2 (N:P:K) ratio.
Physiological Disorder Warning: Fluctuating soil moisture coupled with localized calcium deficiency causes Blossom-End Rot (BER) (black, sunken, leathery necrosis at the distal end of the fruit).
Ripening & Physiological Harvest Windows (Day 111 – 140+)

Phenology: Chlorophyll breaks down rapidly; lycopene (red pigment) and beta-carotene synthesize; pectin methylesterase and polygalacturonase soften the cell walls; titratable acidity drops while soluble sugars rise.

Thermal Synthesis Limit: Lycopene synthesis stops completely when ambient temperatures exceed 30–32°C (fruit turns pale yellow/orange due to beta-carotene accumulation without developing crimson red).
Harvest Calibration:
Long-Distance Interstate Transport: Picked at Breaker / Turning stage (first hint of pink/tannish-yellow on  of surface).
Local Fresh Markets: Picked at Pink / Light-Red stage (60–90% red surface).
Industrial Processing Cannery: Picked at Full Red-Ripe stage (100% deep crimson, TSS ).

Because commercial capsicum (Capsicum annuum var. grossum Sendtn.) is cultivated under two distinct production architectures—open-field winter plains and climate-controlled naturally ventilated polyhouses (NVPH)—market availability runs continuously across the year. The open-field winter crop provides volume across eastern and central plains, while protected cultivation in Haryana and the Deccan plateau, along with counter-cyclical summer hill flushes in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir, fills warm-weather market gaps.

India exports between 18,000 and 28,000 MT of fresh capsicum (bell peppers) annually. Open-field green bell peppers dominate overland cross-border trade into neighboring countries, while high-value colored bell peppers (red and yellow) grown under protected cultivation move via air-cargo and reefer containers to the Middle East and Southeast Asia
Key Processed Products & Production Breakdown Estimates
Commercial processing of bell pepper absorbs approximately 1.5% to 2.2% of India's gross production (roughly 9,500 to 14,500 MT of fresh crop equivalents annually).

Bell pepper processing requires distinct raw materials: green bell peppers provide herbal notes, crispness, and aroma, while mature red bell peppers are selected for sweetness (high soluble sugars), carotenoid color stability, and thick pericarps. Industrial utilization centers on freezing, gentle dehydration, and acidified brine pickling.

Individually Quick Frozen (IQF) Bell Pepper Dices & Strips: Washed, cored, de-seeded, and mechanically cut into uniform dices (6 mm, 10 mm) or julienne strips (5–7 mm wide); blanched at 85–90°C for 60–90 seconds to inactivate catalase/peroxidase enzymes, and blast-frozen at  in fluidized-bed freezers. Sold as single colors or IQF Tri-Color Pepper Mixes (Green, Red, Yellow) for frozen pizzas, ready-to-eat curries, and export food-service lines.

Dehydrated Bell Pepper Flakes, Granules & Powder: Hot-air belt-dried or solar-tunnel-dried flakes (moisture ); used as visual inclusions and savory flavor components in dry instant noodles, dehydrated soup mixes, seasoning packets, and processed meats.

Preserved & Pickled Bell Peppers in Acidified Brine: Deseeded halves, strips, or roasted whole bell peppers packed in acidified brine ( acetic acid / citric acid + salt) in food-grade barrels or glass jars; exported to European and US foodservice markets.

Fire-Roasted Pepper Puree & Paste: Flame-roasted red bell peppers with char-peeled skins, pureed and thermally sterilized into aseptic bag-in-drum formats; base for continental sauces, dips (muhammara, ajvar), and roasted-pepper soups.

Capsicum Oleoresin & Natural Color Extraction: Solvent-extracted non-pungent oleoresin from dried red sweet bell peppers/paprika types, providing natural carotenoid red coloring (capsanthin and capsorubin) for confectionery, cosmetics, and meat formulations.

Crop Phenology & Climatic Parameters

Capsicum (Capsicum annuum var. grossum) is a sensitive, non-climacteric, day-neutral solanaceous annual (or weak perennial in protected polyhouses). It is far more sensitive to temperature extremes than field chillies or tomatoes: optimal daytime temperatures are 20–25°C, while night temperatures must remain within 16–19°C. Continuous temperatures below 12°C or above 32°C severely inhibit fruit set and induce floral drop.

Detailed Phenological Breakdown
Nursery & Plug Tray Phase (Day 0 – 30)
Phenology: Seeds sown in 98-well pro-trays in sterilized cocopeat + vermiculite + perlite inside 40-mesh insect-proof net houses; germination occurs in 6–9 days; seedlings develop 4–6 true leaves.
Target Caliber: Sturdy seedlings, 12–15 cm tall with a well-developed, non-circling root plug.
Biosecurity Requirement: Mandatory protective netting to prevent vector entry of thrips and aphids, which vector Capsicum Chlorosis Virus (CaCV) and Chilli Veinal Mottle Virus (ChiVMV).
Transplanting & Field Establishment (Day 31 – 45)
Phenology: Seedlings transplanted into raised beds covered with 25–30 micron silver-black reflective plastic mulch with dual drip lateral lines. Spacing:  (paired row) in polyhouses;  in open fields.
Ideal Climate: Soil temperature 18–22°C; daytime ambient 22–26°C.
Root Establishment: Feeder roots establish in the upper 20–25 cm soil horizon; light, frequent drip fertigation prevents water stress.
Active Vegetative Growth & Structural Pruning (Day 46 – 65)
Phenology: Plant exhibits characteristic dichotomous branching (the main stem divides into two equal branches, each dividing again at every subsequent node).

Polyhouse Training: Plants are pruned and trained to a 2-leader or 4-leader trellising system using vertical polypropylene twine attached to overhead GI support wires; lateral shoots are pinched out at every node, retaining only the main flowering branches.

The "Crown Flower" Pruning: The solitary flower appearing at the first main fork (crown bud) is manually removed; leaving the crown flower stunts vegetative framework and severely depresses subsequent commercial yields.
Anthesis, Pollination & Initial Fruit Set (Day 66 – 85)
Phenology: White solitary pendent flowers open at branch axils; flowers are bisexual, self-compatible, but benefit from air movement and vibrating agitation for pollen dehiscence.
Critical Thermal Stress Thresholds:
High Temperature Abscission: Daytime temperatures  or night temperatures  cause stigma exertion, pollen inviability, and 100% blossom drop.
Cold Night Chilling: Night temperatures  cause poor pollen tube growth, resulting in flat, deformed, seedless, button-shaped fruits without commercial value.
Fruit Bulking & Mature Green Stage (Day 86 – 115)

Phenology: Rapid cell division followed by intense cell expansion; pericarp wall thickens (); locular chambers expand, creating the characteristic 3-to-4-lobed blocky shape; seeds mature inside the central placenta.
Nutrient Balance: High potassium () and Calcium () fertigation requirement.

Physiological Disorder Warning: Blossom-End Rot (BER) occurs rapidly if calcium translocation is restricted by dry soil moisture swings or excessive electrical conductivity (EC ). Direct sunlight on exposed fruit walls triggers Sunscald (papery, bleached, sunken patches).
Color Turning to Physiological Harvest Maturity (Day 116 – 140+)

Phenology: For colored peppers (yellow/red), chlorophyll degrades over a 15–25 day window; intense carotenoid accumulation converts green tissue to brilliant yellow (violaxanthin/lutein) or scarlet red (capsanthin/capsorubin); pericarp sugars rise (TSS hits 7–9° Brix).
Harvest Calibration:
Green Table Capsicum: Harvested when fully sized, firm, deep glossy green, with thick walls (Day 85–100).
Colored Bell Peppers: Harvested when 80% to 90% of the pod surface displays the final color (Day 115–135). Fruit is hand-clipped leaving a smooth 1.5–2.0 cm pedicel stub.
Phytosanitary Matrix: Major Pests, Diseases & Management

Bell pepper has delicate epidermal tissue and tender growing tips, making it susceptible to the "murda" leaf-curl pest complex (thrips and mites) and soil-borne fungal pathogens, especially in continuous polyhouse monocultures.
